claim: Enteroendocrine cells are specialized sensory cells of the gut-brain axis that are sparsely distributed along the intestinal epithelium.
source: Enteroendocrine cells are specialized sensory cells of the gut-brain axis that are sparsely distributed along the intestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about enteroendocrine cells, stated in the abstract.

claim: Individual enteroendocrine cells typically produce multiple, sometimes apparently opposing, gut hormones in combination.
source: However, individual enteroendocrine cells typically produce multiple, sometimes apparently opposing, gut hormones in combination, and some gut hormones are also produced elsewhere in the body.
evidence: This is supported by references to prior work and the manuscript's own transcriptomic data showing co-expression patterns.

claim: Some gut hormones are also produced elsewhere in the body.
source: However, individual enteroendocrine cells typically produce multiple, sometimes apparently opposing, gut hormones in combination, and some gut hormones are also produced elsewhere in the body.
evidence: This is established knowledge referenced in the manuscript with citations (Lee and Soltesz, 2011; Okaty et al., 2019).

claim: Vil1-p2a-FlpO knock-in mice restrict reporter expression to intestinal epithelium.
source: We targeted FlpO expression to the endogenous Villin1 locus (in Vil1-p2a-FlpO knock-in mice) to restrict reporter expression to intestinal epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing GFP expression patterns in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Combined use of Cre and Flp alleles effectively targeted major transcriptome-defined enteroendocrine cell lineages.
source: Combined use of Cre and Flp alleles effectively targeted major transcriptome-defined enteroendocrine cell lineages that produce serotonin, glucagon-like peptide 1, cholecystokinin, somatostatin, or glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-color expression analysis and single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of different enteroendocrine cell types variably impacted feeding behavior and gut motility.
source: Chemogenetic activation of different enteroendocrine cell types variably impacted feeding behavior and gut motility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Enteroendocrine cells are first-order chemosensory cells of the gut-brain axis.
source: Enteroendocrine cells are first-order chemosensory cells of the gut-brain axis and are sparsely distributed along the gastrointestinal tract (Gribble and Reimann, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Gribble and Reimann, 2019.

claim: Enteroendocrine cells are electrically excitable.
source: Like taste cells, enteroendocrine cells are epithelial cells with neuron-like features, as they are electrically excitable, release vesicles upon elevation of intracellular calcium, and form synaptic connections with second-order neurons through specialized extrusions called neuropods (Bohórquez et al., 2015; Reimann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bohórquez et al., 2015 and Reimann et al., 2012.

claim: Enteroendocrine cells release vesicles upon elevation of intracellular calcium.
source: Like taste cells, enteroendocrine cells are epithelial cells with neuron-like features, as they are electrically excitable, release vesicles upon elevation of intracellular calcium, and form synaptic connections with second-order neurons through specialized extrusions called neuropods (Bohórquez et al., 2015; Reimann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bohórquez et al., 2015 and Reimann et al., 2012.

claim: Enteroendocrine cells form synaptic connections with second-order neurons through specialized extrusions called neuropods.
source: Like taste cells, enteroendocrine cells are epithelial cells with neuron-like features, as they are electrically excitable, release vesicles upon elevation of intracellular calcium, and form synaptic connections with second-order neurons through specialized extrusions called neuropods (Bohórquez et al., 2015; Reimann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bohórquez et al., 2015 and Reimann et al., 2012.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing approaches revealed a diversity of enteroendocrine cell types that produce different gut hormones.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing approaches revealed a diversity of enteroendocrine cell types that produce different gut hormones (Beumer et al., 2018; Gehart et al., 2019; Haber et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beumer et al., 2018; Gehart et al., 2019; Haber et al., 2017.

claim: There are five major enteroendocrine cell lineages defined by expression of either GIP, ghrelin, serotonin, somatostatin, or a combination of GLP1, CCK, and/or neurotensin.
source: Superimposing cell birthdate on the enteroendocrine cell atlas through an elegant genetically encoded fluorescent clock revealed five major enteroendocrine cell lineages defined by expression of either glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), ghrelin, serotonin (called enterochromaffin cells), somatostatin, or a combination of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP1), cholecystokinin (CCK), and/or neurotensin (Gehart et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gehart et al., 2019.

claim: GLP1 and CCK are satiety hormones released following nutrient intake.
source: GLP1 and CCK are satiety hormones released following nutrient intake, ghrelin is an appetite-promoting hormone whose release is suppressed by nutrients, and serotonin can be released by non-nutritive signals like irritants, force, and catecholamines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gut hormone functions.

claim: Ghrelin is an appetite-promoting hormone whose release is suppressed by nutrients.
source: GLP1 and CCK are satiety hormones released following nutrient intake, ghrelin is an appetite-promoting hormone whose release is suppressed by nutrients, and serotonin can be released by non-nutritive signals like irritants, force, and catecholamines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gut hormone functions.

claim: Serotonin can be released by non-nutritive signals like irritants, force, and catecholamines.
source: GLP1 and CCK are satiety hormones released following nutrient intake, ghrelin is an appetite-promoting hormone whose release is suppressed by nutrients, and serotonin can be released by non-nutritive signals like irritants, force, and catecholamines.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gut hormone functions.

claim: Sugar-induced release of GIP and GLP1 causes the incretin effect which rapidly promotes insulin release and lowers blood glucose.
source: Sugar-induced release of GIP and GLP1 causes the incretin effect which rapidly promotes insulin release and lowers blood glucose (Holst et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holst et al., 2009.

claim: CCK, serotonin, and other gut hormones regulate gut motility, gastric emptying, gastric acidification, absorption, gallbladder contraction, and exocrine pancreas secretion.
source: CCK, serotonin, and other gut hormones additionally regulate a variety of digestive functions, including gut motility, gastric emptying, gastric acidification, absorption, gallbladder contraction, and exocrine pancreas secretion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gut hormone functions.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of enteroendocrine cells in the distal colon which express insulin-like peptide 5 triggers appetite suppression through a peptide YY (PYY) receptor.
source: For example, chemogenetic activation of enteroendocrine cells in the distal colon which express insulin-like peptide 5 triggers a multipronged physiological response that includes appetite suppression through a peptide YY (PYY) receptor, improved glucose tolerance through GLP1, and defecation indirectly through the serotonin receptor HTR3A (Lewis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2020.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of enteroendocrine cells in the distal colon which express insulin-like peptide 5 triggers improved glucose tolerance through GLP1.
source: For example, chemogenetic activation of enteroendocrine cells in the distal colon which express insulin-like peptide 5 triggers a multipronged physiological response that includes appetite suppression through a peptide YY (PYY) receptor, improved glucose tolerance through GLP1, and defecation indirectly through the serotonin receptor HTR3A (Lewis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2020.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of enteroendocrine cells in the distal colon which express insulin-like peptide 5 triggers defecation indirectly through the serotonin receptor HTR3A.
source: For example, chemogenetic activation of enteroendocrine cells in the distal colon which express insulin-like peptide 5 triggers a multipronged physiological response that includes appetite suppression through a peptide YY (PYY) receptor, improved glucose tolerance through GLP1, and defecation indirectly through the serotonin receptor HTR3A (Lewis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2020.

claim: Neurog3-Cre and Neurod1-Cre lines labeled a sparse population of intestinal epithelial cells characteristic of enteroendocrine cells.
source: Neurog3-Cre and Neurod1-Cre lines labeled a sparse population of intestinal epithelial cells characteristic of enteroendocrine cells, although the Neurog3-Cre line additionally labeled other cells in intestinal crypts and in occasional mice produced broad labeling of intestinal epithelium; neither Atoh1-Cre line tested displayed selective labeling of enteroendocrine cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Schonhoff et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Schonhoff et al., 2004.

claim: Neither Atoh1-Cre line tested displayed selective labeling of enteroendocrine cells.
source: Neurog3-Cre and Neurod1-Cre lines labeled a sparse population of intestinal epithelial cells characteristic of enteroendocrine cells, although the Neurog3-Cre line additionally labeled other cells in intestinal crypts and in occasional mice produced broad labeling of intestinal epithelium; neither Atoh1-Cre line tested displayed selective labeling of enteroendocrine cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Schonhoff et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Schonhoff et al., 2004.

claim: Neurod1-Cre mice provide broad, indelible, and selective marking of enteroendocrine cells within the intestine.
source: Neurod1-Cre mice provide broad, indelible, and selective marking of enteroendocrine cells within the intestine, but NeuroD1 is also expressed in a variety of other tissues, including the brain, retina, pancreas, peripheral neurons, and enteric neurons (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E; Cho and Tsai, 2004; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E, and citations to Cho and Tsai, 2004; Li et al., 2011.

claim: NeuroD1 is expressed in the brain, retina, pancreas, peripheral neurons, and enteric neurons.
source: Neurod1-Cre mice provide broad, indelible, and selective marking of enteroendocrine cells within the intestine, but NeuroD1 is also expressed in a variety of other tissues, including the brain, retina, pancreas, peripheral neurons, and enteric neurons (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E; Cho and Tsai, 2004; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E, and citations to Cho and Tsai, 2004; Li et al., 2011.

claim: Knockout of NeuroD1 is lethal, causing severe deficits in neuron birth and survival, as well as in the development of pancreatic islets and enteroendocrine cells.
source: Knockout of NeuroD1 is lethal, causing severe deficits in neuron birth and survival, as well as in the development of pancreatic islets and enteroendocrine cells (Gao et al., 2009; Naya et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2009; Naya et al., 1997.

claim: Villin1 (Vil1) is expressed with high selectivity in the lower gastrointestinal tract.
source: Villin1 (Vil1) is expressed with high selectivity in the lower gastrointestinal tract (el Marjou et al., 2004; Maunoury et al., 1992), so we generated a knock-in mouse allele (Vil1-p2a-FlpO) that drives FlpO recombinase expression from the endogenous Vil1 locus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to el Marjou et al., 2004; Maunoury et al., 1992.

claim: Vil1-p2a-FlpO mice displayed expression of a Flp-dependent Gfp allele in epithelial cells throughout the entire length of the intestine with striking specificity.
source: Vil1-p2a-FlpO mice displayed expression of a Flp-dependent Gfp allele in epithelial cells throughout the entire length of the intestine with striking specificity (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reporter expression in Vil1-p2a-FlpO mice was not observed in most tissues examined, including most brain regions, spinal cord, peripheral ganglia, and enteric neurons.
source: Reporter expression was not observed in most other tissues examined, including most brain regions, spinal cord, peripheral ganglia, and enteric neurons; rare GFP-expressing cells were noted in taste papillae, epiglottis, pancreas, liver, and thalamus (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D; Höfer and Drenckhahn, 1999; Madison et al., 2002; Rutlin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D, and citations to Höfer and Drenckhahn, 1999; Madison et al., 2002; Rutlin et al., 2020.

claim: Rare GFP-expressing cells in Vil1-p2a-FlpO mice were noted in taste papillae, epiglottis, pancreas, liver, and thalamus.
source: Reporter expression was not observed in most other tissues examined, including most brain regions, spinal cord, peripheral ganglia, and enteric neurons; rare GFP-expressing cells were noted in taste papillae, epiglottis, pancreas, liver, and thalamus (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D; Höfer and Drenckhahn, 1999; Madison et al., 2002; Rutlin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D, and citations to Höfer and Drenckhahn, 1999; Madison et al., 2002; Rutlin et al., 2020.

claim: Combining Neurod1-Cre and Vil1-p2a-FlpO alleles yielded highly selective expression of an intersectional reporter gene in enteroendocrine cells.
source: Combining Neurod1-Cre and Vil1-p2a-FlpO alleles (Neurod1INTER) yielded highly selective expression of an intersectional reporter gene encoding tdTomato (Rosa26CAG-lsl-fsf-tdTomato herein defined as inter-tdTomato) in enteroendocrine cells, with only occasional cells observed in pancreas, and no detectable expression in other cell types labeled by either allele alone (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Twenty-five percent of Neurog3-lineage cells expressed classical markers for enteroendocrine cells.
source: Twenty-five percent of Neurog3-lineage cells (1454/5856) and 87% of NeuroD1-lineage cells (1595/1841) expressed classical markers for enteroendocrine cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Eighty-seven percent of NeuroD1-lineage cells expressed classical markers for enteroendocrine cells.
source: Twenty-five percent of Neurog3-lineage cells (1454/5856) and 87% of NeuroD1-lineage cells (1595/1841) expressed classical markers for enteroendocrine cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The full diversity of known enteroendocrine cell types was similarly captured by both Neurog3-Cre and Neurod1-Cre lines.
source: Moreover, the full diversity of known enteroendocrine cell types was similarly captured by both Cre lines, with Neurog3-Cre mice additionally labeling many other cells, including paneth cells, goblet cells, enterocytes, and progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neurog3-Cre mice additionally labeled paneth cells, goblet cells, enterocytes, and progenitors.
source: Moreover, the full diversity of known enteroendocrine cell types was similarly captured by both Cre lines, with Neurog3-Cre mice additionally labeling many other cells, including paneth cells, goblet cells, enterocytes, and progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NeuroD1 acts later than Neurogenin3 in the enteroendocrine cell lineage, but prior to cell fate decisions leading to enteroendocrine cell specialization.
source: These findings are consistent with NeuroD1 acting later than Neurogenin3 in the enteroendocrine cell lineage, but prior to cell fate decisions leading to enteroendocrine cell specialization (Jenny et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by citation to Jenny et al., 2002.

claim: Selective clustering analysis of 3049 enteroendocrine cells revealed 10 distinct cell clusters.
source: Selective clustering analysis of 3049 enteroendocrine cells from both mouse lines revealed 10 distinct cell clusters, with one cluster representing putative progenitors (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There are three classes of enterochromaffin cells that similarly express serotonin biosynthesis enzymes (Tph1) and associated transcription factors (Lmx1a), but differentially produce Tac1, Cartpt, Pyy, Ucn3, and Gad2.
source: We observed three classes of enterochromaffin cells that similarly express serotonin biosynthesis enzymes (Tph1) and associated transcription factors (Lmx1a), but differentially produce Tac1, Cartpt, Pyy, Ucn3, and Gad2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: L, I, and N cells are thought to be derived from a common cell lineage.
source: Six other cell types preferentially express either Gip (K cells), Cck (I cells), Gcg (GLP1 precursor, L cells), Nts (N cells), Sst (D cells), and Ghrl (X cells), with L, I, and N cells thought to be derived from a common cell lineage (Beumer et al., 2020; Gehart et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beumer et al., 2020; Gehart et al., 2019.

claim: Enteroendocrine cells detect sugars through the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 (encoded by the gene Slc5a1), with sodium co-transport thought to lead directly to cell depolarization.
source: For example, enteroendocrine cells detect sugars through the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 (encoded by the gene Slc5a1), with sodium co-transport thought to lead directly to cell depolarization (Gorboulev et al., 2012; Reimann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gorboulev et al., 2012; Reimann et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of Slc5a1 was highest in K, L, D, and N cells.
source: Expression of Slc5a1 was observed in multiple enteroendocrine cell subtypes, and highest in K, L, D, and N cells, while abundant expression of T1Rs was not detected in any enteroendocrine cell type (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Abundant expression of T1Rs was not detected in any enteroendocrine cell type.
source: Expression of Slc5a1 was observed in multiple enteroendocrine cell subtypes, and highest in K, L, D, and N cells, while abundant expression of T1Rs was not detected in any enteroendocrine cell type (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Taste blind mice lacking T1Rs can develop a preference for sugar-rich foods through SGLT1-mediated post-ingestive signals of the gut-brain axis.
source: These findings are consistent with the ability of taste blind mice lacking T1Rs to develop a preference for sugar-rich foods through SGLT1-mediated post-ingestive signals of the gut-brain axis (Sclafani et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sclafani et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2020.

claim: Free fatty acid receptor genes Ffar1 and Ffar4 were broadly expressed in several enteroendocrine cell lineages, but largely excluded from enterochromaffin cells.
source: In addition, free fatty acid receptor genes Ffar1 and Ffar4 were broadly expressed in several enteroendocrine cell lineages, but largely excluded from enterochromaffin cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The toxin receptor gene Trpa1 was enriched in enterochromaffin cells.
source: Orthogonally, the toxin receptor gene Trpa1 was enriched in enterochromaffin cells (Bellono et al., 2017), but not abundantly expressed in other enteroendocrine cells (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-cell RNA sequencing shown in Figure 2B and D, and citation to Bellono et al., 2017.

claim: Enterochromaffin cells sense force through the mechanosensory ion channel PIEZO2.
source: Enterochromaffin cells also reportedly sense force through the mechanosensory ion channel PIEZO2 (Alcaino et al., 2018); Piezo2 transcript was not readily detected in our transcriptomic data, but is enriched in enteroendocrine cells from colon that we did not analyze (Billing et al., 2019; Treichel et al., 2022; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alcaino et al., 2018; Billing et al., 2019; Treichel et al., 2022, and experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Each of the seven intersectional combinations produced sparse labeling of intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Each of these seven intersectional combinations produced sparse labeling of intestinal epithelial cells, as expected for labeling of enteroendocrine cell subtypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Striking selectivity for enteroendocrine cells was observed across analyzed tissues for intersectional combinations targeting D, K, L, and I cells.
source: Striking selectivity for enteroendocrine cells was observed across analyzed tissues for intersectional combinations targeting D, K, L, and I cells; sparse labeling was rarely observed in gastric endocrine cells and pancreatic islets, and absent from all other tissues examined.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from tissue analysis.

claim: Tac1INTER and Npy1rINTER alleles more broadly labeled rectal epithelium.
source: We did note that Tac1INTER and Npy1rINTER alleles more broadly labeled rectal epithelium, and Npy1rINTER additionally labeled taste cells as well as rare cells in the airways and epiglottis (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3B.

claim: Npy1rINTER additionally labeled taste cells as well as rare cells in the airways and epiglottis.
source: We did note that Tac1INTER and Npy1rINTER alleles more broadly labeled rectal epithelium, and Npy1rINTER additionally labeled taste cells as well as rare cells in the airways and epiglottis (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3B.

claim: SstINTER mice showed enriched targeting of somatostatin cells throughout the intestine.
source: SstINTER mice showed enriched targeting of somatostatin cells throughout the intestine (SstINTER cells in duodenum, jejunum, ileum, colon, and rectum: 98.9, 66.4, 66.0, 82.4, and 66.0% express somatostatin, 0.3, 0.0, 0.0, 0.8, and 0.0% express serotonin, 0, 0, 0, 0, and 0% express CCK, and 0, 0, 0.9, 2.3, 0% express GLP1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-color expression analysis.

claim: PetINTER driver captured cells with multiple hormones, suggesting that some enteroendocrine cells can either transiently or durably express markers of multiple lineages or can switch identity from enterochromaffin cells to other enteroendocrine cell types.
source: The PetINTER driver also captured cells with other hormones, suggesting that some enteroendocrine cells can either transiently or durably express markers of multiple lineages or can switch identity from enterochromaffin cells to other enteroendocrine cell types (PetINTER cells in duodenum, jejunum, ileum, colon, and rectum: 6.3, 2.0, 4.6, 0.9, and 0% express somatostatin, 86.7, 47.9, 43.7, 52.5, and 49.4% express serotonin, 8.2, 6.5, 3.7, 0.3, and 0.6% express CCK, and 4.6, 17.2, 45.7, 18.5, and 25.7% express GLP1).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from two-color expression analysis.

claim: GcgINTER mice labeled the majority of GLP1 cells.
source: GcgINTER mice did not effectively label either somatostatin or serotonin cells (GcgINTER labeled in duodenum, jejunum, ileum, colon, and rectum 75.5, 67.6, 89.4, 95.9, and 99.0% of GLP1 cells, 34.8, 50.0, 0, 0, and 0% of CCK cells, 0.0, 0.0, 20.8, 34.3, and 22.2% of somatostatin cells, and 1.5, 0.2, 1.8, 0, and 0.8% of serotonin cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from two-color expression analysis.

claim: PetINTER and SstINTER cells were most enriched in the duodenum and colon.
source: PetINTER and SstINTER cells were most enriched in the duodenum and colon (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: GipINTER cells were enriched proximally, with almost no tdTomato+ cells observed in distal intestine.
source: GipINTER cells and GcgINTER cells displayed strikingly distinct spatial patterns. GipINTER cells were enriched proximally, with almost no tdTomato+ cells observed in distal intestine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: GcgINTER cells were present along the entire proximal-distal axis and were enriched in colon and rectum.
source: In contrast, GcgINTER cells were present along the entire proximal-distal axis and were enriched in colon and rectum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neurogenin3 point mutations in human infants or intestine-targeted Neurog3 knockout cause loss of enteroendocrine cells, severe malabsorptive diarrhea, and increased mortality.
source: Hints come from Neurogenin3 point mutations in human infants or intestine-targeted Neurog3 knockout, which cause loss of enteroendocrine cells, severe malabsorptive diarrhea, and increased mortality (Mellitzer et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mellitzer et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2006.

claim: CNO-induced activation of enteroendocrine cells in Neurod1INTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice accelerated gut transit.
source: In control animals lacking DREADD expression, the leading edge of charcoal dye traversed part of the intestine (littermate controls lacking Neurod1-Cre: 22.6 ± 1.2 cm; littermate controls lacking Ptf1a-Cre: 22.8 ± 2.0 cm) (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1). Chemogenetic activation of all enteroendocrine cells in Neurod1INTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice accelerated gut transit, with the charcoal leading edge traversing 30.8 ± 1.5 cm of the intestine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: When DREADD signaling was activated in all epithelial cells using Vil1-Cre; lsl-hM3Dq mice, gavaged dye failed to enter the intestine at all.
source: When DREADD signaling was instead activated in all epithelial cells using Vil1-Cre; lsl-hM3Dq mice, gavaged dye failed to enter the intestine at all (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CNO-accelerated gut transit was not observed in Ptf1aINTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice containing DREADD expression only in pancreatic cells.
source: CNO-accelerated gut transit was not observed Ptf1aINTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice (22.6 ± 2.6 cm) containing DREADD expression only in pancreatic cells (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The net effect of activating all enteroendocrine cells is to promote gut transit.
source: Based on these observations, the observed effects in Neurod1INTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice are due to enteroendocrine cells rather than pancreatic cells, and the net effect of activating all enteroendocrine cells is to promote gut transit.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from chemogenetic experiments.

claim: Pet1INTER cells promoted gut transit.
source: Pet1INTER cells promoted gut transit (Pet1INTER: 29.8 ± 1.6 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 22.1 ± 1.5 cm), while SstINTER and GipINTER cells had no significant effect (SstINTER: 24.5 ± 2.0 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 18.8 ± 1.6 cm; GipINTER: 23.2 ± 1.0 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 22.0 ± 1.8 cm).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: SstINTER and GipINTER cells had no significant effect on gut transit.
source: Pet1INTER cells promoted gut transit (Pet1INTER: 29.8 ± 1.6 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 22.1 ± 1.5 cm), while SstINTER and GipINTER cells had no significant effect (SstINTER: 24.5 ± 2.0 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 18.8 ± 1.6 cm; GipINTER: 23.2 ± 1.0 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 22.0 ± 1.8 cm).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Accelerated gut transit was observed upon chemogenetic activation of Tac1INTER cells but not Npy1rINTER cells.
source: Interestingly, single-cell transcriptome data revealed multiple subtypes of enterochromaffin cells, and we observed accelerated gut transit upon chemogenetic activation of Tac1INTER cells (Tac1INTER: 36.2 ± 1.4 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 21.0 ± 1.1 cm) but not Npy1rINTER cells (Npy1rINTER: 21.8 ± 2.0 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 24.3 ± 2.1 cm).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each enterochromaffin cell subtype may privately communicate with different downstream extrinsic and/or enteric neurons to control gut physiology.
source: These findings raise the possibility that each enterochromaffin cell subtype may privately communicate with different downstream extrinsic and/or enteric neurons to control gut physiology.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential effects of activating different enterochromaffin cell subtypes.

claim: CckINTER and GcgINTER cells slowed gut motility.
source: In contrast, CckINTER and GcgINTER cells slowed gut motility (CckINTER: 7.1 ± 0.3 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 21.5 ± 2.8 cm; GcgINTER: 7.9 ± 0.7 cm, Cre-negative littermates: 22.4 ± 1.9 cm).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neural circuits that mediate toxin responses may achieve priority over those that mediate nutrient responses, at least under conditions of equal and maximal activation.
source: Simultaneous activation of both pathways, as done in Neurod1INTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice, masks the slowing of gut transit by CckINTER and GcgINTER cells. These findings suggest a hierarchy where neural circuits that mediate toxin responses may achieve priority over those that mediate nutrient responses, at least under conditions of equal and maximal activation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data from chemogenetic experiments.

claim: CNO-induced activation of enteroendocrine cells in Neurod1INTER; inter-hM3Dq-mCherry mice caused a 26% reduction in food intake.
source: Animals lacking DREADD expression, or with sparse DREADD expression only in pancreas, ate robustly (~1 g of food over a 2 hr period). In contrast, CNO-induced activation of enteroendocrine cells caused a 26% reduction in food intake (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of enterochromaffin cells reduced feeding behavior by 52.1%.
